items.text: Price $30 minus COGS and shipping $18 gives $12 per subscriber per month, a 40% margin. Value is measured on this margin, not on revenue.
Customer acquisition cost is marketing spend divided by new subscribers in the same period. Example: $90,000 over 1,500 new subscribers gives $60.
Lifetime value is margin per month times expected lifetime: $12 × 12.5 ≈ $150.
LTV/CAC is about 2.5 here, below the rule-of-thumb minimum of 3 before scaling paid acquisition.
Payback is CAC divided by monthly margin: $60 / $12 = 5 months. Each new subscriber is a cash outflow for those 5 months.
Expected lifetime in months ≈ 1 / monthly churn. At 8% churn that is about 12.5 months.
Cutting churn from 8% to 6% raises lifetime to about 16.7 months and LTV to about $200.
Early churn is usually much higher than later churn. A single average rate hides it, so read cohort retention curves.
Computing LTV on revenue overstates value by 2.5× here (30 / 12).
With a 5-month payback, LTV/CAC can look healthy while growth still drains cash. Check payback next to LTV/CAC.
Measure CAC per channel and per cohort, not blended. A blended figure hides an expensive channel behind a cheap one.
Build retention by signup cohort to see first-month drop-off separately from later churn.

items.anchor: Price test on a traffic share
items.text: Test a price rise to $33 for new subscribers on part of the traffic before rolling it out. This is a margin lever.
Marketing wants to double paid ads. CAC tends to rise with spend because the cheapest audiences are reached first, and LTV/CAC is already below 3 at 8% churn.
Churn levers: annual prepaid plan with discount, skip-a-month button. Margin lever: price rise to $33 for new subscribers. Measurement: CAC by channel and cohort.

open_doubts: Is the annual plan's discount worth the lower margin, given that it also brings the cash forward?
